pos: n. (Faustus of Riez, c. 405–c. 490, abbot of Lérins and bishop of Riez in Provence, whose treatise On Grace gave classic form to the view later called Semi-Pelagianism)
etymology: Latin faustus, fortunate; Riez is in Provence. Not to be confused with Faustus of Milevis, the Manichee, or Faustus Socinus.
biblical_def: Faustus of Riez was a Briton by birth who became abbot of the famous island monastery of Lérins and then bishop of Riez. He was a strict ascetic, a defender of the Trinity against the Arian Visigoths who exiled him, and a man of real piety. In the 470s a presbyter named Lucidus taught a hard predestinarianism, and Faustus had him condemned at the Synod of Arles. He then wrote On Grace, arguing that grace always helps, but that the will retains a native power to begin to seek God, which grace then rewards and strengthens. Fulgentius and later the Second Council of Orange answered him from Scripture: “no man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father” (Joh 6:65); faith itself is a gift, “unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him” (Php 1:29); “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8). The opening of the heart is the Lord's, as with Lydia, “whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul” (Act 16:14). Faustus is honoured as a saint in Provence; his doctrine was condemned at Orange in 529.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grace, in theology, as the free unmerited love and favour of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
webster_full: GRACE, n. Favour; good will; kindness.
2. Appropriately, the free unmerited love and favour of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
scriptures: Joh 6:65
And he said, Therefore said I unto you, that no man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father.
Php 1:29
For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake;
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
corruption_summary: Faustus was a holy man with a reasonable doctrine, and that combination is why Semi-Pelagianism has always been the church's most comfortable error.
corruption_paragraphs: Faustus did not deny grace or the need of it. He opposed a predestinarian extreme and wanted to preserve human responsibility. Most modern evangelicals would find his position congenial, even orthodox: God gives grace to all, and those who respond with their own first step receive more. The ascetic seriousness of Lérins and the moderation of his views made him a figure the church could admire.

The recovery is Orange's answer, which the Reformation restored and the 1689 Confession confesses: the natural man is not able by his own strength to convert himself or to prepare himself thereunto. The gift is not only grace to help the believing; it is the believing itself. The Lord opened Lydia's heart before she attended.
roots_summary: Greek didomi (G1325), to give; charizomai (G5483), to give freely; dianoigo (G1272), to open.
roots_lines: Greek charizomai (G5483) — to grant as a favour; Philippians 1:29.
Greek dianoigo (G1272) — to open thoroughly; Acts 16:14, Luke 24:45.
usage: “except it were given unto him of my Father” (Joh 6:65) — against the native beginning of faith.
“unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him” (Php 1:29) — faith itself a gift.
“whose heart the Lord opened” (Act 16:14) — the order Faustus reversed.

pos: n. (Hincmar, c. 806–882, archbishop of Reims, the most powerful churchman of the Carolingian West, who had Gottschalk flogged and imprisoned and opposed his doctrine of twofold predestination)
etymology: Germanic personal name. Archbishop of Reims from 845; a formidable canonist and administrator.
biblical_def: Hincmar was archbishop of Reims for nearly forty years and the leading prelate of the Frankish church. When Gottschalk taught twofold predestination, Hincmar had him condemned at the Synod of Quierzy in 849, flogged until he cast his writings into the fire, and confined at the monastery of Hautvillers for the rest of his life. At a second synod at Quierzy in 853 Hincmar issued four chapters: one predestination only, of the elect to life; God wills all men to be saved; Christ suffered for all; the free will lost in Adam is restored by grace. He pressed Paul's word that God “will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth” (1Ti 2:4), but passed over the Shepherd's own definition of His death: “I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15), and His high-priestly prayer, “I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me” (Joh 17:9). Prudentius of Troyes, Ratramnus and the Council of Valence (855) opposed his chapters. His treatment of Gottschalk, who died refusing to recant, fell under James's sentence: “he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy” (Jas 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prelate as an ecclesiastic of a higher order, as an archbishop, bishop or patriarch; a dignitary of the church.
webster_full: PRELATE, n. An ecclesiastic of a higher order, as an archbishop, bishop or patriarch; a dignitary of the church.
scriptures: Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.
As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.
Joh 17:9
I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine.
Jas 2:13
For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.
corruption_summary: Hincmar defended a universal redemption and a single predestination by flogging the monk who disagreed, and his doctrine is now the evangelical default while his methods are forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapters of Quierzy read like a modern statement of moderate evangelical soteriology: God wills all to be saved, Christ died for all equally, election is to life only, and no one is predestined to perdition. They were imposed by the most powerful archbishop in Europe on a monk who appealed to Augustine and Scripture. The contrast between the moderation of the doctrine and the brutality of its enforcement is a lesson of its own.

The 1689 Confession confesses particular redemption: to all those for whom Christ hath obtained eternal redemption, He doth certainly and effectually apply and communicate the same. Christ's intercession is for those given Him, and His death for His sheep. The recovery is that doctrine, held with the mercy Hincmar did not show.
roots_summary: Greek thelo (G2309), to will; tithemi (G5087), to lay down; erotao (G2065), to pray, ask.
roots_lines: Greek tithemi psuchen — to lay down one's life; John 10:11, 15.
usage: “Who will have all men to be saved” (1Ti 2:4) — Hincmar's proof text at Quierzy.
“I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15) — the Shepherd's own definition.
“judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy” (Jas 2:13) — Hautvillers.

pos: n. (Rabanus Maurus, c. 780–856, abbot of Fulda and archbishop of Mainz, called the Teacher of Germany, who refused Gottschalk's release from Fulda and condemned him at Mainz in 848)
etymology: Latin Hrabanus, from Germanic hraban, raven; Maurus was the name given him by his teacher Alcuin, after St Benedict's disciple. The hymn Veni Creator Spiritus is traditionally ascribed to him.
biblical_def: Rabanus Maurus was Alcuin's best pupil and for twenty years the head of the school of Fulda, which he made the great centre of learning east of the Rhine. He wrote commentaries on almost every book of Scripture, a manual for the training of clergy, and an encyclopedia of the natural world read allegorically. The hymn Come, Creator Spirit, long sung at ordinations and in Reformed and Lutheran churches in translation, is traditionally his; its prayer is Christ's promise, “the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things” (Joh 14:26), and “how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?” (Luk 11:13). As abbot he refused the young Gottschalk, an oblate placed in the monastery as a child, the release a synod had granted him, and as archbishop of Mainz in 848 he condemned Gottschalk's doctrine and sent him to Hincmar. He also wrote against Paschasius Radbertus's identification of the sacramental body with the historical body. His legacy is mixed: a teacher who served the church's learning, and a prelate who used his office against a man who appealed to Augustine.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines teacher as one who teaches or instructs; an instructor; and, in Scripture, one who teaches the gospel; a minister.
webster_full: TEACHER, n. One who teaches or instructs.
2. One who instructs others in religion; a preacher; a minister of the gospel.
scriptures: But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.
If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: Rabanus is honoured as a Carolingian educator; the Gottschalk affair shows how learning in the service of an institution can be turned against the doctrine it was meant to serve.
corruption_paragraphs: The Carolingian schools did immense good, preserving texts and training clergy, and Rabanus stood at their centre. But his learning was harnessed to the order of the monastery and the hierarchy, and when a monk wished to leave the vow his father had made for him, and later taught a doctrine of grace the hierarchy disliked, the teacher of Germany became his judge. The pattern recurs in every institution, Reformed ones included, that values its order above the consciences of the men in it.

The recovery is learning that serves the Word and the church's freedom under it. The prayer of Veni Creator is the right prayer for every teacher: that the Spirit teach and lead into truth, and that no office be used to silence an appeal to Scripture.
roots_summary: Greek parakletos (G3875), Comforter; didasko (G1321), to teach; aiteo (G154), to ask.
usage: “he shall teach you all things” (Joh 14:26) — the prayer of Veni Creator.
“give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him” (Luk 11:13) — the hymn's warrant.
“commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2) — the schoolmaster of Fulda.

pos: n. (Prudentius of Troyes, d. 861, Spanish-born bishop of Troyes who defended Gottschalk's twofold predestination against Hincmar and John Scotus Eriugena)
etymology: Latin prudens, prudent; his Spanish name was Galindo. Not to be confused with Aurelius Prudentius, the fourth-century Christian poet.
biblical_def: Prudentius of Troyes was a Spaniard who served at the court of Louis the Pious and became bishop of Troyes about 843. When Gottschalk was condemned, Prudentius wrote in his defence and against John Scotus Eriugena, whom Hincmar had enlisted and who argued that predestination to punishment was impossible because evil is nothing. Prudentius answered from Augustine and Scripture that God has predestined some to life by mercy and others to just punishment, not to sin, as Paul writes of “the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction” (Rom 9:22) and “the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory” (Rom 9:23). He held that Christ's redeeming blood was shed for the elect, citing the Lord's own words to the unbelieving, “ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep” (Joh 10:26). He refused to sign Hincmar's chapters of Quierzy, and his views found support at the Council of Valence in 855. Paul's golden chain was his foundation: “whom he did predestinate, them he also called” (Rom 8:30). He is a witness that in the ninth century the Augustinian doctrine had bishops as well as a persecuted monk on its side.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reprobation as the act of disallowing with detestation; and, in theology, the predestination of certain persons to destruction, or the decree of God passing by those not elected.
webster_full: REPROBATION, n. The act of disallowing with detestation, or of expressing disapprobation.
2. In theology, the predestination of certain persons to destruction.
scriptures: Rom 9:22
What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction:
Rom 9:23
And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory,
But ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep, as I said unto you.
Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
corruption_summary: Prudentius shows that the doctrine of reprobation was defended in the medieval church by sober bishops, not invented by Calvin, and that its defenders carefully separated God's decree from the cause of sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern objection treats reprobation as a cruelty peculiar to Calvinism. Prudentius held it six centuries before Calvin, and he held it carefully: God predestines the wicked to the punishment their sins deserve, not to the sins themselves, and passes them by in justice while saving others in mercy. Eriugena's clever argument that evil is nothing, and so cannot be predestined, made a philosophical point at the expense of Paul's plain words about vessels of wrath.

The 1689 Confession confesses the same distinction: the rest of mankind God was pleased to pass by and to ordain them to dishonour and wrath for their sin, to the praise of His glorious justice. The recovery is to hold the doctrine as Prudentius did — reverently, from the text, without making God the author of sin.
roots_summary: Greek skeuos (G4632), vessel; katartizo (G2675), to fit, prepare; proetoimazo (G4282), to prepare beforehand.
roots_lines: Greek katartizo (G2675) — to fit, make ready; Romans 9:22.
Greek proetoimazo (G4282) — to prepare beforehand; Romans 9:23, Ephesians 2:10.
usage: “the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction” (Rom 9:22) — the half of the doctrine Eriugena denied.
“the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory” (Rom 9:23) — the other half.
“ye are not of my sheep” (Joh 10:26) — Prudentius on the extent of redemption.

pos: n. (Claudius of Turin, d. c. 827, Spanish-born bishop of Turin who removed images and crosses from his churches and opposed pilgrimages, relic-veneration and the invocation of saints)
etymology: Latin Claudius, a Roman family name. Not to be confused with the emperor Claudius or Claudius Lysias of Acts 23.
biblical_def: Claudius of Turin was a Spaniard trained in the Augustinian tradition who wrote commentaries on Paul for the emperor Louis the Pious and was made bishop of Turin about 816. Finding the churches of his diocese full of images to which the people bowed, he had them removed, crosses included, and preached against the veneration of relics, the invocation of saints and pilgrimages to Rome. To those who said they honoured the cross because Christ hung on it, he answered that by the same reasoning they should adore mangers, boats and asses, since Christ had been laid in one, sailed in another and ridden on the third. His warrant was the law: “Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them” (Exo 20:5), and Christ's word, “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24). When men honoured a saint, he pointed to Peter refusing Cornelius's homage: “Stand up; I myself also am a man” (Act 10:26). Writers such as Dungal and Jonas of Orléans attacked him, but he kept his see until his death. John's last line was his whole programme: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1Jn 5:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines iconoclast as a breaker or destroyer of images; a name given by the Romanists to those who reject the use of images in religious worship.
webster_full: ICONOCLAST, n. A breaker or destroyer of images; a name given by the Romanists to those who reject the use of images in religious worship.
scriptures: Exo 20:5

Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
But Peter took him up, saying, Stand up; I myself also am a man.
Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen.
corruption_summary: Claudius shows that opposition to images in worship was alive in the Western church of the ninth century, a fact that the charge of Protestant novelty conveniently forgets.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome and Orthodoxy present image veneration as the settled faith of the church since Nicaea II, and the Reformation's iconoclasm as an aberration. A ninth-century bishop of Turin, protected by a Carolingian emperor, removed the images from his churches and argued against them from Scripture, and the Frankish church at Frankfurt had already rejected Nicaea's decree. The supposed consensus was a Roman and Byzantine one.

The recovery is the second commandment as a rule of worship, confessed by the 1689 Confession: God may not be worshipped by images or any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture. Claudius's argument about mangers and asses is still a good one. The object Christ touched is not thereby an object of worship; only Christ is.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachah (H7812), to bow down; Greek proskuneo (G4352), to worship; eidolon (G1497), idol.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachah (H7812) — to bow down, prostrate oneself; Exodus 20:5.
Greek proskuneo (G4352) — to worship, do reverence; John 4:24, Acts 10:25.
usage: “Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them” (Exo 20:5) — the law Claudius enforced at Turin.
“Stand up; I myself also am a man” (Act 10:26) — his answer to the cult of the saints.
“Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1Jn 5:21) — the programme of his episcopate.

pos: n. (Agobard, c. 769–840, archbishop of Lyons, who wrote against trial by ordeal and combat, against the belief that sorcerers raise storms, and against the veneration of images)
etymology: Germanic personal name. Archbishop of Lyons from 816.
biblical_def: Agobard was born in Spain and became archbishop of Lyons, where he wrote a series of short treatises remarkable for their age. Against the Frankish custom of trial by ordeal and judicial combat he argued that it tempts God to demand a miracle at men's convenience, and that God does not promise to vindicate the innocent in that way: “Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God” (Deu 6:16). Against the popular belief that weather-makers summoned hailstorms and that ships from a land called Magonia carried away the stolen crops, he wrote that rain and hail are in God's hand, who “saith to the snow, Be thou on the earth” (Job 37:6), and “covereth the heaven with clouds, who prepareth rain for the earth” (Psa 147:8). He opposed images in churches in the same spirit as Claudius of Turin, and treated the dabbling in charms forbidden by the law, which names any “that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter” (Deu 18:10), as a denial of God's providence. Agobard also wrote harsh treatises against the Jews of Lyons and against their standing at court, and in politics he sided with the sons of Louis the Pious in their rebellion; the Reformed reader honours his reasoning from Scripture against superstition without approving either.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ordeal as an ancient form of trial to determine guilt or innocence, by fire or water, practised by the rude nations of Europe.
webster_full: ORDEAL, n. An ancient form of trial to determine guilt or innocence, practised by the rude nations of Europe, and still practised in the East Indies.
scriptures: Deu 6:16
Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah.
Job 37:6
For he saith to the snow, Be thou on the earth; likewise to the small rain, and to the great rain of his strength.
Who covereth the heaven with clouds, who prepareth rain for the earth, who maketh grass to grow upon the mountains.
There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,
corruption_summary: Agobard's attack on ordeals and weather-magic is an early Christian argument that Scripture's doctrine of providence, not modern scepticism, is what frees men from superstition.
corruption_paragraphs: The common story is that superstition was dispelled by the Enlightenment and science. Agobard dismantled the ordeal and the weather-sorcerer in the ninth century by an appeal to God's sovereignty: God does not perform on demand, and storms are not sold by sorcerers but sent by the Lord. A world governed by providence is a world where charms are useless and fear of sorcerers is foolish.

The recovery is the 1689 Confession's doctrine of providence, by which God upholds, directs, disposes and governs all creatures and actions. Modern superstitions — horoscopes, lucky charms, manifesting, the fear of curses — are answered the same way. Agobard's other writings show that a man can reason well against one error and fall into another; his reasoning from Scripture is what is worth keeping.
roots_summary: Hebrew nasah (H5254), to tempt, prove; sheleg (H7950), snow; qesem (H7081), divination.
roots_lines: Hebrew nasah (H5254) — to test, try, tempt; Deuteronomy 6:16.
usage: “Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God” (Deu 6:16) — Agobard against the ordeal.
“For he saith to the snow, Be thou on the earth” (Job 37:6) — against the weather-makers.
“who prepareth rain for the earth” (Psa 147:8) — providence, not sorcery.

pos: n. (Vigilantius, fl. c. 400, presbyter of Gaul who wrote against the veneration of relics, night vigils at martyrs' tombs, candles lit by day and prayers to the saints, and was savagely attacked by Jerome)
etymology: Latin, ‘watchful,’ from vigilans. Jerome mocked him as Dormitantius, the sleepy one.
biblical_def: Vigilantius was a presbyter from Calagurris in southern Gaul who visited Jerome at Bethlehem and came home troubled by what he had seen of the growing cult of the martyrs. He wrote that Christians should not venerate the bones of the dead in costly vessels, kiss them, light candles before them in broad daylight, keep all-night vigils at their tombs, or pray to the saints as though the dead could hear. The dead, the Preacher says, “know not any thing” (Ecc 9:5) of what is done under the sun, and there is “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). Paul and Barnabas had refused worship at Lystra: “Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you” (Act 14:15). Christ seeks worshippers who “shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:23). Jerome replied in 406 with Against Vigilantius, written, he boasted, in a single night, full of abuse rather than argument. Vigilantius's book is lost and is known only through Jerome's attack. The Reformers saw in him a witness that the cult of relics was resisted from its beginning.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines relic as that which remains; and, in the Romish church, the body or some part of the body of a deceased saint or martyr, or some part of his clothes or something belonging to him, preserved and held in veneration.
webster_full: RELIC, n. That which remains; that which is left after the loss or decay of the rest.
2. The body or corpse of a deceased person.
3. In the Romish church, the body or some part of the body of a deceased saint or martyr, or some part of his clothes, preserved and held in veneration.
scriptures: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
Ecc 9:5
For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten.

And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:
Joh 4:23
But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him.
corruption_summary: Jerome's reply to Vigilantius is the classic case of abuse taking the place of argument, and of a great scholar defending a practice that Scripture nowhere commands.
corruption_paragraphs: Jerome was the greatest biblical scholar of his age, and against Vigilantius he offered almost no Scripture, only scorn, threats and the appeal to custom. The episode is instructive because the practice he defended — relics, vigils, candles, invocation of the saints — grew into the whole medieval cult of the saints, and because Jerome's prestige carried it. Learning and holiness do not make a practice Scriptural.

The 1689 Confession confesses that religious worship is to be given to God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and to Him alone; not to angels, saints or any other creatures, and that since the fall not without a Mediator, nor in the mediation of any other but Christ alone. Vigilantius said as much in a single treatise and was called a sleepy fool for it.
roots_summary: Greek mesites (G3316), mediator; Greek homoiopathes (G3663), of like passions; alethinos proskunetes, true worshipper (G228, G4353).
roots_lines: Greek homoiopathes (G3663) — of like nature, like passions; Acts 14:15, James 5:17.
Greek proskunetes (G4353) — a worshipper; John 4:23, the only use.
usage: “one mediator between God and men” (1Ti 2:5) — against the invocation of saints.
“We also are men of like passions with you” (Act 14:15) — the apostles refusing worship.
“worship the Father in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:23) — against candles by day at the tombs.

pos: n. (Jovinian, d. c. 405, Roman monk who taught that married believers are not lower in merit than virgins, that fasting is no better than eating with thanksgiving, and that the regenerate are kept by God; condemned at Rome and Milan c. 390)
etymology: Latin Jovinianus, from Jovis, of Jove. Known chiefly through Jerome's Against Jovinian (393).
biblical_def: Jovinian was himself a monk and lived unmarried, but he taught at Rome that virgins, widows and married women who have been baptized into Christ are of equal standing, if they do not differ in other works. He said that abstaining from food is no holier than eating it with thanksgiving, that there is one reward in heaven for all the faithful, and that those who have been born again with full faith cannot be overthrown by the devil. Scripture is on his side on each point: “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled” (Heb 13:4); Paul calls it a doctrine of devils to be “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3), “For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:4); and John writes that the one born of God “cannot sin, because he is born of God” (1Jn 3:9), that is, cannot go on in sin as his life. Pope Siricius condemned him about 390, Ambrose did the same at Milan, and Jerome attacked him with a book so extreme in its disparagement of marriage that Jerome's own friends tried to withdraw it from circulation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines celibacy as an unmarried state; a single life; especially that of a bachelor, or of a man or woman who has made a vow not to marry.
webster_full: CELIBACY, n. An unmarried state; a single life; especially that of a bachelor, or of a man or woman who is bound by vows not to marry.
scriptures: Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:
Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin; for his seed remaineth in him: and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.
corruption_summary: Jovinian was condemned for saying that marriage is not a lower Christian state than virginity, and the Reformation, which said the same, was accused of his heresy.
corruption_paragraphs: The fourth-century church was moving rapidly toward a two-tier Christianity in which the celibate and ascetic were spiritually superior, and Jovinian challenged it from Scripture. His condemnation helped fix the ranking for a thousand years, with consequences for clerical celibacy, the monastic vow and the low estimate of the married layman. When Luther and the Reformers married and taught the holiness of the household, their opponents called them Jovinianists.

The 1689 Confession confesses marriage as God's ordinance for all sorts of people who are able with judgment to give their consent, and forbids no lawful marriage to any calling. Jovinian's other teachings, on the equal standing of the faithful and the keeping power of God, point toward the Reformation's doctrines of justification and perseverance. The recovery is to receive his witness on marriage and food plainly, as Paul gave it.
roots_summary: Greek timios (G5093), honourable, precious; koluo (G2967), to forbid; eucharistia (G2169), thanksgiving.
usage: “Marriage is honourable in all” (Heb 13:4) — Jovinian's first proposition.
“Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” (1Ti 4:3) — the error he resisted.
“every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused” (1Ti 4:4) — against fasting as merit.

pos: n. (Aerius of Sebaste, fl. c. 360, presbyter of Pontus who taught that a bishop and a presbyter are of one order, rejected prayers and offerings for the dead, and refused fixed fasts; listed by Epiphanius among the heretics)
etymology: Greek Aerios, from aer, air. Known almost entirely from Epiphanius's Panarion, chapter 75.
biblical_def: Aerius was a presbyter and the manager of a hospice for the poor at Sebaste, a friend of the bishop Eustathius until a quarrel when Eustathius was preferred over him. He then taught three things that put him among the heretics in Epiphanius's catalogue. First, that a bishop differs in nothing from a presbyter, for Paul calls the same men elders and bishops: Titus was to “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5), “For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God” (Tit 1:7), and Paul greets the church at Philippi “with the bishops and deacons” (Php 1:1), naming no third order. Second, that prayers and offerings for the dead are useless, since “it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27). Third, that fixed fasts and the Easter observance should not be imposed as law. His followers were driven from the churches and met in the fields. Epiphanius thought his first point madness. Jerome, who held a similar view of the original identity of bishop and presbyter, was never called a heretic for it. The Reformed churches, Presbyterian and Baptist alike, have since confessed what Aerius said on all three points.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines presbyter as an elder; a person somewhat advanced in age, who has authority in the church; a priest or minister.
webster_full: PRESBYTER, n. In the primitive Christian church, an elder; a person somewhat advanced in age, who had authority in the church, and whose duty was to feed the flock over which the Holy Spirit had made him overseer.
2. A priest; one who has the pastoral or parochial charge.
scriptures: Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Tit 1:7
For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;
Php 1:1
Paul and Timotheus, the servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons:
Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
corruption_summary: Aerius was catalogued as a heretic for teaching what the New Testament plainly says about elders and bishops, and his case shows how early church custom was treated as apostolic law.
corruption_paragraphs: By the late fourth century the bishop had become a distinct and higher order over the presbyters, and prayers for the dead were universal. Epiphanius could not imagine that a presbyter who denied either was anything but a heretic. Yet the New Testament uses presbuteros and episkopos of the same men, and nowhere commands prayer for the departed. The equation of custom with apostolic tradition is the root of every later Roman claim.

The 1689 Confession confesses that the officers appointed by Christ for the church are bishops or elders, and deacons, and that prayer is to be made for the living, but not for the dead. Aerius's quarrel with his bishop may have sharpened his views, but the views themselves are the Bible's. The recovery is to test custom by Scripture, however ancient the custom.
roots_lines: Greek episkopos (G1985) — overseer, bishop; Titus 1:7, Philippians 1:1, Acts 20:28.
usage: “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) — elders and bishops one office.
“with the bishops and deacons” (Php 1:1) — no third order at Philippi.
“once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27) — against prayers for the dead.

pos: n. (Helvidius, fl. c. 380, Roman layman who argued from Scripture that Mary bore other children after Jesus and that marriage is not inferior to virginity; answered by Jerome's Against Helvidius, 383)
etymology: Latin family name. His treatise is lost and known only through Jerome's reply.
biblical_def: Helvidius was a Roman Christian layman who, against the growing exaltation of virginity, wrote that Mary and Joseph lived as husband and wife after Jesus' birth and had other children, the ‘brethren of the Lord’ named in the Gospels. He read Matthew's words plainly, that Joseph “knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son” (Mat 1:25), and the neighbours' question at Nazareth, “is not his mother called Mary? and his brethren, James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas?” (Mat 13:55), “And his sisters, are they not all with us?” (Mat 13:56). Paul calls one of them “James the Lord's brother” (Gal 1:19). Helvidius drew the further point that a holy married life is not a lower form of Christian devotion. Jerome answered with Against Helvidius, arguing that the brethren were cousins and that Mary remained a virgin perpetually. The question touches no article of salvation, and many of the Reformers held the perpetual virginity as a pious opinion. But Scripture never teaches it, and its later use — to exalt Mary above the ordinary state of believing women and to rank celibacy above marriage — is the error Helvidius saw coming.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines virginity as maidenhood; the state of having had no carnal knowledge of man.
webster_full: VIRGINITY, n. Maidenhood; the state of having had no carnal knowledge of man.
scriptures: Mat 1:25
And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS.
Is not this the carpenter's son? is not his mother called Mary? and his brethren, James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas?
And his sisters, are they not all with us? Whence then hath this man all these things?
Gal 1:19
But other of the apostles saw I none, save James the Lord's brother.
corruption_summary: The perpetual virginity of Mary became a support for the medieval exaltation of Mary and of celibacy, and Helvidius's plain reading of the Gospels was its first challenge.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of the perpetual virginity was not an idle speculation. It belonged to a theology in which sexual union within marriage was thought to compromise holiness, and in which Mary was increasingly set apart from all other women as an object of devotion. Rome now teaches it as dogma and Orthodoxy as settled tradition. Helvidius's case rested on the plain sense of Matthew and Paul, and Jerome's reply rested on a theory of cousins the texts do not suggest.

The Reformed reader honours Mary as the blessed mother of our Lord, the believing handmaid of the Lord, without adding to Scripture. The 1689 Confession binds no conscience beyond the Word. The recovery is the plain reading of the Gospels, and the honour of the Christian household in which Mary and Joseph, by every natural reading, raised the Lord's brothers and sisters.
roots_summary: Greek ginosko (G1097), to know, of marital union; prototokos (G4416), firstborn; adelphos (G80), brother.
roots_lines: Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know, used of marital union; Matthew 1:25.
usage: “knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son” (Mat 1:25) — Helvidius's first text.
“his brethren, James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas” (Mat 13:55) — the household at Nazareth.
“James the Lord's brother” (Gal 1:19) — Paul's plain description.
